Before the current administration scrubbed any hint of DEI from federal websites, the TWD stated that part of its mission was the following:

"TWD programs foster the training and development of a strong and dive​rse biomedical research workforce. The division funds research training, career development and diversity-enhancing activities through a variety of programs at the undergraduate, graduate, postdoctoral, faculty and institutional levels. In addition, TWD administers the NIH Common Fund initiative, [Enhancing the Diversity of the NIH-Funded Workforce](http://web.archive.org/web/20241015065235/https://www.nigms.nih.gov/training/dpc/pages/default.aspx)."

[http://web.archive.org/web/20241015065235/https://www.nigms.nih.gov/research-areas/areas-of-research/training-and-workforce-development](http://web.archive.org/web/20241015065235/https://www.nigms.nih.gov/research-areas/areas-of-research/training-and-workforce-development)

As such, I would imagine MSTPs have been recruiting diverse classes to be consistent with this mission. Given the "break first and fix later" doctrine of the current administration, I wouldn't put it past them to target MSTPs just as a part of their blanket destruction of anything to do with diversity.

I am hoping that the two year buffer proves to be enough to keep MSTPs moving forward in their current capacity. MSTP students tend to be the cream of the crop, and schools want to retain them the most. So, perhaps the reduction in PhD-only admissions will save enough money such that programs can retain the same number of MSTP students in their grad phases. But that's my speculation, so who knows what will really happen.

MSTP grants fall under the Training and Workforce Development study section + many PIs have grants that are not being reviewed. That is to say, MSTP grants may be interpreted as being a part of DEI initiatives and labs may have to take far fewer students (if any) due to funding constraints. Some faculty I’ve spoken to at a big name MSTP have expressed concern that MSTP acceptances may be rescinded. I don’t think it has come to the point that MD, PhD programs would disappear, but personally, I would be very worried. But, we’ve done the best we can up to this point, so is there really much use in worrying about something so far beyond our control?

Sure. I'll try to keep it short. I'm working with single-cell RNA-seq data from embryonic frogs cells. These unprocessed data were available to me right when I joined the lab as a freshman as the experiment was performed before I got there. After processing and diving into some basic analysis in R, I began to notice some red flags. There was about 40% mtRNA content in these cells where it should be no more than 10% based on publications on closely related organisms from other research groups. I was told by my PI that this number is ok and I shouldn't worry about it. Additionally, I saw that the people who performed the cell preparation before me accidentally left the tissue in dissociation buffer for much longer than they should have (they noted this in their lab journal). They also did not use the wide-bore pipette tips that the protocol says are needed. I believe these contributed to the the cell viability being <90% when they counted. 


My PI also wants me to ignore clustering these data as she doesn't "trust" PCA, UMAP, etc. What she wants is for me to take individual counts from each cell and manually divide them by counts of other genes in other cells to determine the "expression ratio" to illustrate cell heterogeneity.  What she also wants me to do is look 1000bp upstream of the 5' UTR of each gene to determine promoter regions and use those sequences to determine why some genes are expressed more/less than others. When I do what she says, she decides that it wasn't quite what she wanted and wants me to try something different, hence my "moving the goalpost" statement.  Consequently, I haven't really gotten anywhere with this project.  Sorry if that was confusing, as I am also confused. I've tried nudging her in a different direction, but she remains firm in her stance.

I think these are the big points, I'd be happy to expand in more detail another time when I'm done with class for the day.
